content: Your doctor has prescribed penicillin, an antibiotic, to treat your infection. This medication will either be injected into a large muscle, such as your buttock or hip, or administered through an intravenous (IV) fluid that drips into your vein via a needle or catheter. The IV infusion typically lasts 30 minutes or more and is given four to six times daily. Penicillin works by eliminating bacteria responsible for various infections, including pneumonia, meningitis, and infections of the skin, bones, joints, stomach, blood, and heart valves. In some cases, penicillin may be prescribed for other conditions; consult your doctor or pharmacist for further details. Your healthcare provider will monitor the effectiveness of the treatment and any potential side effects through laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is crucial to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how well your infection and symptoms respond to the medication. Before starting penicillin, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to penicillin, cephalosporins, or any other medications. Additionally, provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription drugs you are taking, especially other antibiotics, anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like naproxen or ibuprofen, atenolol, diuretics, oral contraceptives, probenecid, and vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have a history of kidney or liver disease, allergies, asthma, blood disorders, colitis, stomach issues, or hay fever. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. Should you become pregnant while taking penicillin, contact your doctor immediately. If you have diabetes and routinely check your urine for sugar, use Clinistix or TesTape, as penicillin can cause false-positive results with Clinitest tablets. Before administering penicillin, inspect the solution carefully. It should be clear and free of any floating particles. Check the bag or container for leaks by gently squeezing it or observing it closely. Do not use the solution if it appears discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Instead, use a new solution and show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. Follow your healthcare provider’s instructions precisely when using this medication. Do not stop the treatment on your own, as this could worsen your infection and potentially lead to hospitalization. Do not alter your dosing schedule without consulting your healthcare provider. If you encounter a mechanical issue, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, your healthcare provider may advise you to stop the infusion. Penicillin may cause side effects. Minor side effects include an upset stomach and diarrhea. If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your healthcare provider. Severe side effects require immediate medical attention and include rash, itching, fever, chills, facial swelling, wheezing, difficulty breathing, unusual bleeding or bruising, dizziness, seizures, or a sore mouth or throat. If you experience a serious side effect, you or your doctor can report it to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. If you are receiving penicillin intravenously, your healthcare provider will likely supply you with several days’ worth of medication at a time. Store the medication in the refrigerator or freezer as instructed. Remove the next dose from the refrigerator one hour before use and place it in a clean, dry area to allow it to reach room temperature. If you are storing additional penicillin in the freezer, transfer a 24-hour supply to the refrigerator each day. Do not refreeze the medication. If you are receiving penicillin intramuscularly, follow your healthcare provider’s storage instructions carefully. Keep all supplies in a clean, dry place and out of reach of children. Your healthcare provider will also instruct you on how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. If you are receiving penicillin intravenously or subcutaneously, be aware of the signs of a catheter-related infection. Symptoms include tenderness, warmth, irritation, drainage, redness, swelling, and pain near the catheter site. Notify your healthcare provider immediately if you experience any of these symptoms. The brand name for this medication is Pfizerpen®.
